## One line to start

```{r, eval=FALSE}
library(bloomr)
bloom_map("nj")
```

1. Select **Bloom counties** to expand New Jersey.
2. Select a county, then choose **Bloom municipalities**.
3. Drag an area if it overlaps another. Its dot remains at the original position.
4. Select **Back** to return one level.

The return to the county view animates both the map and the camera. The
original county lines remain in the state map, and original municipality
lines remain in the county. Both can be turned off with the **Display** button.
Labels are off by default; hover for names. Dark mode is optional; light
is the default.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
bloom_map("tx", theme = "dark")
```

## Color counties using your data

```{r, eval=FALSE}
rates <- data.frame(
  geoid = c("34003", "34013", "34021"),
  rate = c(12.5, 18.2, 9.3)
)

bloom_check_data(rates, value = "rate")
bloom_map("nj", data = rates, key = "geoid", value = "rate")
```

GEOIDs must be character strings, including any leading zeros. Each ID appears
once. Values must be numeric. Rows without a value appear in gray when the
corresponding geography has data.

## Where it works

Use `bloom_map()` in the RStudio Viewer or an HTML report. For Shiny, use
`bloomOutput()` and `renderBloom()`, explained in the
[Shiny guide](using-in-shiny.html). Local data comes with the package, so it
does not call an online geographic service at runtime.

## Before using your own geography

Version 0.1.0 ships prepared NJ and TX data. It does not yet read arbitrary
`sf` or GeoJSON boundaries. You can add *numeric data* by geographic ID, but
not replace the base geography.

Standalone HTML output must include its widget dependency folder and be tested
on its final hosting setup. Single-file self-contained HTML publishing is not
yet verified.
